title: Financial Inclusion and Consumer Protection Policy
summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers widen access to financial services while protecting consumers through strategy, regulation, redress and fraud prevention.
intro: This training programme equips ministries, legislators and public agencies to design policy that widens access to financial services while protecting consumers: inclusion strategies, digital finance, financial literacy, consumer protection frameworks, redress and the fight against fraud and scams.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give policymakers a practical understanding of how to expand access to useful, affordable financial services and how to protect consumers once they use them. Participants leave able to design a national financial inclusion strategy, strengthen the consumer protection framework, set up effective complaints and redress arrangements, and respond to the growing threat of fraud and scams.
sections.What It Covers: Measuring financial access and exclusion, national financial inclusion strategies, digital financial services and mobile money, digital identity and proportionate customer due diligence, financial literacy and capability strategies, consumer protection frameworks and institutional models, complaints handling and ombudsman schemes, fraud and scams, and evaluating policy impact.
Intended Audience: Officials in finance ministries, treasuries and central banks responsible for financial inclusion and consumer policy
Staff of consumer protection agencies, ombudsman schemes and financial education bodies
Legislative drafters, legal advisers and parliamentary committee staff working on consumer and financial inclusion legislation
Learning Objectives: Measure financial access, usage and exclusion and identify the groups most affected
Design a national financial inclusion strategy with clear targets and governance
Assess the opportunities and risks of digital financial services for inclusion
Develop a national financial literacy and capability strategy
Evaluate consumer protection frameworks, institutional models and redress arrangements
Design a coordinated policy response to fraud and scams
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over two to three days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with country case studies and policy exercises, ending in a strategy workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the government's priorities.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some familiarity with financial services, social or consumer policy is helpful. No technical background in financial regulation is required.
Core Reading: G20/OECD (2022), High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
World Bank (2017), Good Practices for Financial Consumer Protection
OECD (2020), Recommendation of the Council on Financial Literacy
CPMI and World Bank (2016), Payment Aspects of Financial Inclusion
World Bank (2022), The Global Findex Database 2021: Financial Inclusion, Digital Payments, and Resilience in the Age of COVID-19

modules.title: Financial Inclusion: Evidence and Barriers
modules.summary: Why financial inclusion matters for growth and resilience, how access and usage are measured, and the economic, social and regulatory barriers that keep people excluded.
objectives: Explain the economic and social case for financial inclusion
Use demand-side and supply-side data to measure access and usage
Identify the barriers facing women, rural, low-income and other excluded groups
syllabus: Inclusion, growth, resilience and poverty reduction
Global Findex and national survey data
Barriers: cost, distance, documentation, trust and capability
Gender gaps, small businesses and forcibly displaced people

modules.title: National Financial Inclusion Strategies
modules.summary: How to develop, govern and implement a national financial inclusion strategy, setting priorities and targets and aligning ministries, regulators and the private sector.
objectives: Design the structure, priorities and targets of a national strategy
Establish governance and coordination for implementation
Monitor progress with a results framework
syllabus: Diagnostics, stakeholder engagement and priority setting
Governance: steering committees, working groups and secretariats
Public sector levers: government payments, postal networks and state banks
Results frameworks, targets and reporting

modules.title: Digital Finance, Mobile Money and Digital Public Infrastructure
modules.summary: How mobile money, agent networks, digital identity and fast payment systems have transformed access, and the regulatory choices that enable them while managing new risks.
objectives: Explain how digital financial services expand access
Assess enabling regulation for e-money, agents and digital credit
Evaluate the role of digital identity and proportionate customer due diligence
syllabus: Mobile money, agent networks and interoperability
Digital credit, buy now pay later and over-indebtedness
Digital identity, tiered due diligence and FATF guidance on inclusion
Digital public infrastructure and government-to-person payments

modules.title: Financial Literacy and Capability Strategies
modules.summary: How to design a national strategy to improve financial literacy and capability, what evidence shows about what works, and how to reach different audiences effectively.
objectives: Explain the OECD framework for national financial literacy strategies
Assess the evidence on effective financial education interventions
Design programmes for schools, adults, small businesses and vulnerable groups
syllabus: National strategy design, governance and stakeholder roles
Measuring financial literacy and capability
Behavioural insights and teachable moments
Digital financial literacy and scam awareness

modules.title: Consumer Protection Frameworks and Institutions
modules.summary: The legal and institutional foundations of financial consumer protection, the international principles that guide them, and the choices in assigning responsibilities to regulators.
objectives: Explain the G20/OECD High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
Compare institutional models for financial consumer protection
Assess gaps in disclosure, fair treatment, product and conduct rules
syllabus: Disclosure, transparency of costs and fair treatment
Responsible lending, product governance and suitability
Institutional models: integrated, twin peaks and dedicated agencies
Data protection, privacy and vulnerable consumers

modules.title: Complaints, Redress and Ombudsman Schemes
modules.summary: How to give consumers effective routes to redress, from internal complaints handling to independent ombudsman schemes, and how complaints data can inform policy and supervision.
objectives: Set standards for internal complaints handling by firms
Design an independent, accessible and fair ombudsman scheme
Use complaints data to identify emerging harm
syllabus: Internal dispute resolution standards
Ombudsman scheme design: independence, jurisdiction, funding and binding decisions
Mass redress, collective actions and compensation schemes
Complaints data as an early warning system

modules.title: Fraud, Scams and Consumer Harm
modules.summary: The rapid growth of authorised push payment fraud, investment scams and online financial harm, and the policy tools to prevent fraud, allocate liability and support victims.
objectives: Describe the main fraud and scam typologies affecting consumers
Evaluate prevention, reimbursement and liability allocation policies
Design coordination between regulators, law enforcement, telecoms and online platforms
syllabus: Investment, romance, impersonation and authorised push payment scams
Reimbursement and liability models for payment fraud
Online platforms, telecoms and advertising controls
National fraud strategies and victim support

modules.title: Balancing Inclusion, Protection and Innovation
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining the trade-offs between inclusion, protection, stability and integrity, and building an integrated policy action plan.
objectives: Weigh trade-offs between inclusion, consumer protection and financial integrity
Evaluate policy impact using evidence and data
Produce an integrated inclusion and consumer protection action plan
syllabus: Proportionality and the inclusion, stability, integrity and protection balance
Sandboxes and innovation in inclusive finance
Impact evaluation and course correction
Workshop: an inclusion and consumer protection action plan
